name: Magical thinking
statement: Magical thinking is reasoning by contact and by resemblance: juice a sterilised cockroach has touched stays spoiled, and fudge moulded as dog faeces stops being food.
meaning: Three different things travel under this name and they do not share an evidence base. The anthropological sense is Frazer's and Mauss's, two laws abstracted from ritual practice in traditional cultures: contagion, once in contact always in contact, and similarity, the image equals the object. The clinical sense is a symptom dimension, measured by the Magical Ideation Scale and the Thought-Action Fusion Scale, and studied in obsessive-compulsive disorder and the schizophrenia spectrum. The experimental sense is a set of laboratory demonstrations that ordinary educated adults act on both laws when food and disgust are involved. This entry's verdict covers the third. The experimental claim is about behaviour, not doctrine. Rozin and his colleagues argued that people who reject the cockroach juice know it is safe and say so. They reject it anyway. That is why the paper describes the effects as operating at gut level rather than as beliefs anyone would defend.

origin.who: Paul Rozin, Linda Millman and Carol Nemeroff
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Frazer and Mauss named the two laws at the turn of the twentieth century to describe ritual in traditional cultures. The 1986 paper took them into a laboratory room in Philadelphia and tested them on Americans, which is the move that made the idea a psychological finding rather than an ethnographic one.

evidence: Fifty people from the University of Pennsylvania community sat through a single session, 17 men and 33 women, aged 17 to 50 with a mean of 23.6, about half of them students. Each rated items on a 200 mm line anchored at 'dislike extremely' and 'like extremely'. A dried, sterilised cockroach about 4 cm long was dropped into a glass of juice, stirred for five seconds and removed with a new spoon; a plastic birthday candleholder went into the other glass as a control. Ratings of the roached juice fell 102 points against 3 points for the control, a net drop of 98.82 with a standard deviation of 71.62, p < .001, in the predicted direction for 46 of 49 subjects. Fudge moulded into the shape of dog faeces was rated 47.18 points below the same fudge shaped as a disc, and rubber imitation vomit 49.26 points below a rubber sink stopper. Two bottles of sucrose were labelled by the experimenter, one Sucrose and one Sodium Cyanide, with the subject told in advance that both held sugar. Forty-one of 50 preferred to drink from the sucrose bottle, a mean gap of 30.58 points, and only one subject suggested the cyanide bottle might actually hold cyanide. When subjects stuck the labels on themselves the gap fell to 16.5 points, t = 2.60, p < .02. That test ran on 38 subjects rather than 50, because 12 were dropped on the strength of their first cyanide result. Forty-seven subjects threw darts at photographs: accuracy dropped 11.32 mm for John F. Kennedy and 11.02 mm for the face of the person they liked most, p < .02 in both cases. The paper also reports the measures that did not work. Darts at Hitler and at a disliked person moved 2.11 mm and 4.91 mm, neither reaching significance. A toothbrush used by the person the subject was most attracted to was predicted to gain value and lost it, 19.68 points in the wrong direction, p < .01. Serving fresh juice of the kind that had been roached moved ratings 11.33 points, t = 1.74, p < .05 one-tailed, with only 30 of 49 subjects going the predicted way.

examples.tag: The coat that belonged to someone terrible
examples.text: A charity shop jumper turns out to have belonged to a man convicted of something awful. It has been cleaned twice and nobody will wear it. Asked whether the wool carries anything, the same people say no, and they still will not put it on.

A plain ring worth very little is treated as irreplaceable because she wore it for fifty years. An identical ring bought new would not do, which is the same rule about contact running in the pleasant direction.

A cake is decorated with a fat marzipan slug, and guests who watched the sugar go in eat around it. They know what it is made of and can say so. The resemblance is enough to stop the fork, which is the law of similarity doing work in a kitchen.

replication.headline: Contagion reappears among Hadza hunter-gatherers and Tannese subsistence farmers, at a mean rejection rate of 94% for contaminated food, but no preregistered direct replication of the 1986 session was located.
replication.detail: Apicella and colleagues ran contagion scenarios with Hadza hunter-gatherers in Tanzania and Tannese subsistence farmers on Vanuatu. Hyena meat, a cough and arrow poison each briefly entered a pot of honey or of boiling broth and were then removed. Fifty-one Hadza judged the three contaminants in 2013; 66 more judged a bead from a headband in 2014. Mean rejection across the three contaminants was 94% for both foods, against 68% for the bead. Six Fisher's exact tests separated contaminants from the bead, all at p < 0.001. On Tanna, 63 participants across three age bands judged eight scenarios involving a pot of yams. Endorsement of eating ran at 0.16 of 4 contaminated items against 0.98 of 4 control items, F(1, 63) = 36.11, p < 0.0001, partial eta-squared 0.367, with no effect of age, F(2, 60) = 2.40, p = 0.099. Hejmadi, Rozin and Siegal put the same task to 125 Hindu Indian and 106 American children. Once the contaminant had been taken out again, 4- to 5-year-olds rejected the juice 64.5% of the time on average and 8-year-olds 89.5%. With the contaminant still present, 59 of 82 Indian 4- to 5-year-olds rejected all three contaminants against 33 of 75 Americans, chi-square(1, N = 157) = 11.93, p < .001. An independent consumer laboratory found the same thing without disgust at full strength. Morales and Fitzsimons gave 95 undergraduates a shopping basket in which feminine napkins either did or did not touch a package of cookies. Quality ratings of the cookies fell from 6.99 to 5.34, F(1, 91) = 20.22, p < .001. Rozin later put the properties to a Prolific sample of 198 American residents on 11 and 12 June 2020, asking about the coronavirus. His tables report 195. Asked how many viruses would have to reach their lungs to give them a 50% chance of catching COVID-19, 110, or 56%, answered one. Told that a bottle of 1,000 viruses had sat on a laboratory shelf for a year, 87, or 45%, reported no drop in discomfort at all.

study.cite: Apicella, C. L., Rozin, P., Busch, J. T. A., Watson-Jones, R. E., & Legare, C. H. (2018). Evidence from hunter-gatherer and subsistence agricultural populations for the universality of contagion sensitivity. Evolution and Human Behavior, 39(3), 355-363.

limits: No effect sizes are printed in the structured fields, because nothing measures the same quantity twice. The original reports millimetre shifts on a rating line, the cross-cultural work reports rejection rates, and pairing them would invent a comparison neither paper makes. The verdict covers negative contagion in the food and disgust domain, which is the part of the 1986 paper that later work has gone back to. Positive contagion and the dart-throwing test of similarity were weak or reversed in the original itself and no replication of either was located. Rozin is an author on both the cross-cultural study and the developmental one, so these are extensions by the founding laboratory rather than independent tests; Morales and Fitzsimons is the one independent demonstration used here. Apicella and colleagues do not claim their populations are innocent of germ theory. They record that some Hadza attend school and a few mentioned germs, that 46% of their Tannese participants gave a germ explanation at least once, and that knowledge of germ theory in these groups has yet to be tested directly. Searches on 21 September 2026 of Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC and the Open Science Framework registration index found no preregistered direct replication of Rozin, Millman and Nemeroff. The nearest item is a student project in the Hagen Cumulative Science Project replicating study 3 of Fedotova and Rozin. Its preregistration at osf.io/cywes is public and dated 29 July 2018, its public components stop at a pre-data report, and no result is posted, so it is not used. Two arithmetic problems in the sources are worth flagging. Apicella and colleagues print F(1, 63) for an analysis whose other tests carry 60 error degrees of freedom. Their figures here were read from the published Elsevier version and matched against the author manuscript in PubMed Central, which agree. Hejmadi and colleagues describe 44 of 82 children as 72%, a percentage that belongs to the preceding paragraph, so only their contaminant-present figures are quoted above. Rozin, Markwith and Ross's 1990 follow-up on labels reading 'not sodium cyanide' is named rather than described. OpenAlex, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar all mark it open and all point to one SAGE file, which returned a Cloudflare bot challenge rather than a paywall on 21 September 2026. Europe PMC holds no record of it, Rozin's own publications page lists the citation without a file, and the Internet Archive is closed to this session. Eckblad and Chapman's 1983 scale paper was not obtained either, its PubMed record carrying no abstract and PsycNet, ResearchGate and Academia.edu each returning a bot challenge on the same date.
misreadings: The three senses get quoted as one body of evidence. Eddy's review of 191 studies found the Thought-Action Fusion Scale in 101 of them and the Magical Ideation Scale in 26, and none of that literature measures whether anyone will drink the cockroach juice. A high magical ideation score is a marker on the psychosis spectrum. Chapman and colleagues followed 508 people for ten years. The 182 who scored high on the Perceptual Aberration Scale, the Magical Ideation Scale or both exceeded 153 controls on psychotic disorders, psychotic relatives, schizotypal symptoms and psychotic-like experiences. That result does not separate the magical ideation scale from the aberration scale. The scale is not a measure of the effects described above, and the two literatures share no instrument. The developmental story is told backwards as often as not. Eddy records magical thinking as a normal part of childhood between the ages of 2 and 7 that fades. Nemeroff and Rozin write that contagion is grown into rather than grown out of, absent below age 4 and first appearing at 4 or 5. Both can be true because they are about different things, and a page that treats them as one construct has the arrow pointing the wrong way half the time. Reading the 1986 paper as a finding about superstition also inverts its argument. Its subjects said the juice was safe, could not explain their refusal, and were embarrassed by it. The paper is usually cited as though all fourteen measures in its Table 1 worked. Two, the dart throws at Hitler and at a disliked person, did not, and the lover's-toothbrush result came out backwards. Tempting fate, entry 17, is a magical-thinking judgement of a narrower kind, and its evidence does not carry over. Many Labs 2 recovered its classroom scenario at d = 0.18 across 8,000 people, while Many Labs 5 found neither that effect nor the cognitive-load interaction it tested. A sterilised cockroach costs a glass of juice half the rating scale.

Morales, A. C., & Fitzsimons, G. J. (2007). Product contagion: changing consumer evaluations through physical contact with 'disgusting' products. Journal of Marketing Research, 44(2), 272-283. Study 1 figures read from Fitzsimons's copy at people.duke.edu; the article is closed at the publisher.

Rozin, P. (2023). Magical contagion beliefs operate in reactions of Americans to COVID-19. Judgment and Decision Making, 18, e13. Open access; figures read from the publisher's PDF and confirmed on a second download.

Nemeroff, C., & Rozin, P. (2018). Back in touch with contagion: some essential issues. Journal of the Association for Consumer Research, 3(4), 612-624. Full text read from Rozin's University of Pennsylvania publications page. The later review by the original authors, and the source for the eight properties of contagion and for the claim that it appears at age 4 or 5.

Eddy, C. M. (2026). The many manifestations of magical thinking: a systematic review. Frontiers in Psychiatry, 17, 1759906. Open access; full text read. The source for the counts of instruments across 191 studies and for the clinical sense of the term.

Eckblad, M., & Chapman, L. J. (1983). Magical ideation as an indicator of schizotypy. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology, 51(2), 215-225. The paper the Magical Ideation Scale comes from. Its Crossref and PubMed records carry no abstract, and PsycNet, ResearchGate and Academia.edu each returned a bot challenge on 21 September 2026, so the article itself is unread and nothing is quoted from it.

Chapman, L. J., Chapman, J. P., Kwapil, T. R., Eckblad, M., & Zinser, M. C. (1994). Putatively psychosis-prone subjects 10 years later. Journal of Abnormal Psychology, 103(2), 171-183. Read as the PubMed abstract; the full text was not obtained.

Bibliographic record verified at Crossref. Three indexes mark it open and all point to one SAGE file, which returned a Cloudflare bot challenge on 21 September 2026, so the article is unread and nothing is quoted from it.

Full text read from Rozin's University of Pennsylvania publications page. Target of the one preregistered replication located, osf.io/cywes under project osf.io/4vz39, which posts no result.
